title: Thickness optimization on 20-layer HfO2/SiO2 alternating stack for UV-block/SWIR-pass filtering
scientific_hypothesis: A 20-layer alternating HfO2/SiO2 stack with optimized individual thicknesses can simultaneously achieve high UV reflection (200-400nm) and high SWIR transmission (800-1500nm) on fused silica substrate, with performance improving as thickness perturbations explore wider bounds around the current best candidate.
design_principle: Recalled thin-film interference theory: alternating high/low index layers create Bragg-like reflection bands where optical thickness equals quarter-wavelength multiples. UV blocking requires thinner layers (shorter wavelength), while SWIR transmission requires the stack to be anti-reflective at longer wavelengths. The refractive index contrast between HfO2 (~2.0-2.1 in visible) and SiO2 (~1.45-1.5) provides sufficient modulation for band separation.
proposed_topology: Air | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | HfO2 | SiO2 | Fused Silica substrate (20 layers total, alternating starting with HfO2)
design_variables: Individual layer thicknesses for all 20 layers, with perturbation bounds of ±0.8 nm around the current best candidate's thickness vector
soft_objectives: Maximize target_score combining UV reflection and SWIR transmission
Keep all layers physically realizable (positive thickness, manufacturable range)
manufacturing_considerations: Total layer count fixed at 20 (within 30-layer limit)
All thicknesses should remain in 20-200nm range for practical deposition
Alternating sequence preserved for process simplicity
theory_basis: Recalled principle: quarter-wave stacks produce high reflection at wavelengths where optical thickness equals λ/4 multiples
Recalled principle: index contrast between HfO2 and SiO2 enables bandgap formation in reflection spectrum
Recalled rule of thumb: UV-blocking layers typically 25-50nm physical thickness for 200-400nm band
Recalled expectation: SWIR transmission improves when stack appears optically thin at 800-1500nm wavelengths
expected_advantages: Fixed topology isolates thickness as the only optimization variable
20 layers provides sufficient degrees of freedom within manufacturing constraints
Alternating sequence is deposition-friendly and reduces process complexity
Wider perturbation bounds (±0.8nm vs ±0.5nm) may escape local optima causing round-to-round oscillation
known_risks: Uncertain whether 20 layers is optimal vs 24 or 28 layers - this route does not test layer count
Recalled refractive indices may differ from actual catalog values at UV wavelengths - HfO2 absorption in deep UV is uncertain from memory
Exact quarter-wave thickness calculation depends on dispersion data I have not verified
Wider perturbation bounds may produce non-manufacturable thickness variations if optimizer overshoots
What would settle this: look up HfO2 extinction coefficient at 200-300nm, verify SiO2 dispersion in SWIR band
execution_request_english: Optimize a 20-layer planar dielectric stack on fused silica substrate with air incidence. Materials: alternating hfo2 and SiO2 (Rodriguez-de_Marcos) layers, starting with hfo2 adjacent to air. Design variables: all 20 individual layer thicknesses, initialized from the current best candidate thickness vector with perturbation bounds of ±0.8 nm. Wavelength bands: maximize reflection at 200-400 nm, maximize transmission at 800-1500 nm. Normal incidence, unpolarized light. Total layers fixed at 20. Use gradient_thickness optimizer. Keep all thicknesses positive and within 20-200 nm range.
revision_reason: Continuation of control route with increased perturbation bounds from ±0.5 nm to ±0.8 nm as directed by feedback, anchored to current best candidate thickness vector to maintain focus on validated high-performance region while granting optimizer sufficient degrees of freedom to bypass shallow optical-path barriers.
